chapters.summary: This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jesus Christ’s genealogy from Abraham through David to Joseph, noting the Babylonian captivity and three groups of fourteen generations. It describes Mary’s pregnancy before living with Joseph, Joseph’s plan to divorce her privately, and an angel’s dream instructing him to take Mary and name the child Jesus, citing the Emmanuel prophecy. Joseph obeys and refrains from relations until Jesus is born.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records wise men from the east coming to Jerusalem seeking the newborn King of the Jews, following a star to Bethlehem, and presenting gifts to Jesus with Mary. Herod consults priests and scribes, then orders the killing of Bethlehem’s children. Warned in dreams, the wise men avoid Herod, Joseph flees with Jesus to Egypt, later returns after Herod’s death, and settles in Nazareth in Galilee.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records John the Baptist preaching repentance in the wilderness of Judea, baptizing in the Jordan as people confess sins, and warning Pharisees and Sadducees to produce worthy fruit. John describes one coming after him who baptizes with the Holy Ghost and fire and brings judgment. Jesus comes from Galilee, is baptized by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a heavenly voice identifies Jesus as God’s beloved Son.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jesus being led by the Spirit into the wilderness, fasting forty days, and resisting three temptations by the devil, after which angels minister to him. It covers Jesus departing to Galilee after John is imprisoned, dwelling in Capernaum, preaching repentance and the kingdom of heaven, calling Peter, Andrew, James, and John, and teaching, healing, and drawing crowds from Galilee, Syria, Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judaea, and beyond Jordan.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Jesus teaching on a mountain to his disciples and the multitudes: the Beatitudes; disciples as salt and light; fulfilling the law and prophets; righteousness exceeding scribes and Pharisees; anger and reconciliation; adultery and lust; radical avoidance of sin; divorce and remarriage; forbidding oaths; nonretaliation and generosity; loving enemies, prayer for persecutors, and the command to be perfect.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jesus teaching to give alms, pray, and fast in secret rather than for public display, including the Lord’s Prayer and commands to forgive others. It contrasts earthly and heavenly treasures, discusses the single eye and serving God rather than mammon, and instructs not to be anxious about food, drink, or clothing, but to seek God’s kingdom first.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Jesus’ teachings on not judging others, correcting oneself before others, and not giving holy things to hostile hearers. It covers asking, seeking, and knocking in prayer, the Golden Rule, and entering by the narrow gate. Jesus warns against false prophets known by their fruits, and says only doers of the Father’s will enter. He compares obedience to building on rock; the crowd notes his authority.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jesus cleansing a leper and instructing him to show himself to the priest. In Capernaum Jesus heals a centurion’s servant and speaks of faith and the kingdom. He heals Peter’s mother-in-law and many sick and demon-possessed. He teaches about the cost of following him, calms a storm at sea, casts demons into swine in the Gergesenes, and the city asks him to depart.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jesus returning to his city, forgiving and healing a paralytic amid scribes’ objections, calling Matthew, and eating with publicans and sinners. It addresses fasting with John’s disciples using bridegroom and new cloth/wine sayings. Jesus heals a woman with an issue of blood, raises a ruler’s daughter, gives sight to two blind men, casts out a demon from a mute man, teaches in cities, and urges prayer for laborers.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Jesus naming the twelve apostles, giving them authority to heal and cast out unclean spirits, and sending them to the house of Israel to preach that the kingdom of heaven is at hand. It gives travel and hospitality instructions, warns of rejection and persecution before councils and rulers, urges fearless witness and endurance, notes division in households, calls for taking up the cross, and promises reward for receiving or aiding disciples.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Jesus preaching after instructing the Twelve. John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends disciples to ask if Jesus is the coming one; Jesus cites healings and preaching to the poor. Jesus speaks of John as a prophet and messenger, rebukes this generation’s responses to John and himself, pronounces woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, thanks the Father for revealing to babes, and invites the weary to take his yoke and find rest.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records Jesus defending his disciples’ Sabbath grain picking, healing a man’s withered hand in a synagogue, and Pharisees plotting against him. Jesus heals many and commands silence, with an Isaiah citation. He casts out a demon from a blind, mute man, answers Beelzebub accusations, warns about blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, teaches about words and fruit, refuses a sign except Jonah, describes returning unclean spirits, and identifies doers of God’s will as family.

This chapter contains 58 verses and records Jesus teaching multitudes by the sea in parables: the sower, tares among wheat, mustard seed, leaven, hidden treasure, pearl of great price, and a net. He explains why he uses parables and interprets the sower and tares to the disciples, including end-of-world separation by angels. He returns to his country, faces offense and unbelief, and does few mighty works.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Herod’s imprisonment and beheading of John the Baptist at Herodias’s request, and John’s disciples burying him and informing Jesus. Jesus withdraws to a deserted place, heals the sick, and feeds about five thousand men plus women and children with five loaves and two fishes. Jesus prays alone, walks on the sea, saves Peter, calms the wind, and arrives at Gennesaret where many are healed by touching his garment.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Jesus disputing with Jerusalem scribes and Pharisees about handwashing traditions, citing Isaiah, and teaching that defilement comes from the heart and speech, not food. He explains this to the disciples. In Tyre and Sidon he heals a Canaanite woman’s demon-oppressed daughter. Near the Sea of Galilee he heals many in a mountain setting and then feeds four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish, gathering seven baskets, and departs to Magdala.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Pharisees and Sadducees requesting a sign; Jesus refuses except the sign of Jonah and warns against their “leaven,” explained as their doctrine. In Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ; Jesus speaks of building his church, giving kingdom keys, and commands secrecy. Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection; rebukes Peter. He teaches self-denial, taking up the cross, final judgment, and some seeing the kingdom.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jesus’ transfiguration on a high mountain before Peter, James, and John, with Moses and Elias appearing and a voice from a cloud identifying Jesus. Jesus commands silence until after his resurrection and explains Elias as John the Baptist. He heals a boy possessed by a devil, teaches faith, prayer, and fasting, foretells his betrayal, death, and resurrection in Galilee, and provides tribute money in Capernaum via a coin found in a fish.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jesus teaching that greatness in heaven requires humility like a child, warning against offending “little ones,” and using images of cutting off offending members. It includes the parable of the lost sheep, instructions for resolving a brother’s trespass with witnesses and the church, teachings on binding and loosing and united prayer, and Peter’s question on forgiveness. Jesus gives the parable of the unforgiving servant.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Jesus traveling from Galilee to Judea beyond Jordan, healing multitudes, and answering Pharisees on divorce and remarriage, citing creation and Moses. He speaks of eunuchs, welcomes and blesses little children, and counsels a rich young man to keep commandments, sell possessions, and follow him. Jesus teaches on wealth and salvation, promises rewards and thrones to followers, and states many first are last.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Jesus’ parable of vineyard laborers hired at different hours and paid the same wage, concluding “the last shall be first.” Jesus then predicts his betrayal, condemnation, crucifixion, and resurrection in Jerusalem. The mother of James and John requests places of honor; Jesus teaches servant leadership and his life as a ransom. Leaving Jericho, Jesus heals two blind men who call him Son of David.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem from Bethphage on a donkey amid crowd acclamations, his cleansing of the temple, and healings there. He lodges in Bethany, curses a fruitless fig tree, and teaches about faith and prayer. In the temple he answers questions about authority, gives parables of two sons and wicked husbandmen, and chief priests and Pharisees seek to arrest him but fear the crowd.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Jesus’ parable of the wedding feast, including invited guests refusing, servants slain, the city destroyed, others gathered, and a guest cast out for lacking a wedding garment. It then covers Pharisees and Herodians questioning tribute to Caesar, Sadducees disputing resurrection and marriage, Jesus stating the greatest commandments to love God and neighbor, and Jesus questioning the Pharisees about the Messiah as David’s son and Lord.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Jesus speaking to the crowds and his disciples about scribes and Pharisees: obey their teaching but not their actions. He condemns hypocrisy, self-promotion, burdens on others, misuse of oaths, neglect of judgment, mercy, and faith, and outward purity masking inward wrongdoing. He pronounces woes, foretells persecution of sent messengers, warns judgment on that generation, laments Jerusalem, and declares the house desolate until later acknowledgment.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records Jesus leaving the temple, predicting its destruction, and teaching on the Mount of Olives about signs of his coming and the end: deception, false Christs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, and worldwide preaching. He mentions the abomination of desolation, flight from Judea, great tribulation, cosmic signs, and angels gathering the elect. He urges watchfulness, readiness, and faithful service, warning of judgment on an evil servant.

This chapter contains 46 verses and records Jesus’ parables of the ten virgins awaiting the bridegroom and the servants entrusted with five, two, and one talents, followed by teaching to watch for the Son of man’s coming. It describes final judgment when the Son of man separates nations as sheep and goats, commending acts of mercy and condemning neglect, assigning eternal life or punishment.

This chapter contains 75 verses and records chief priests and elders under Caiaphas plotting to kill Jesus; a woman anoints Jesus in Bethany; Judas agrees to betray him for thirty pieces of silver. Jesus prepares and eats the Passover, predicts betrayal, institutes bread and cup, and foretells Peter’s denial. In Gethsemane Jesus prays and urges watchfulness; Judas leads an armed crowd to arrest him. Jesus is taken to Caiaphas, questioned with false witnesses, condemned, mocked, and Peter denies Jesus three times.

This chapter contains 66 verses and records the chief priests and elders delivering Jesus to Pilate; Judas returning thirty pieces of silver, hanging himself, and the purchase of the potter’s field. Pilate offers Barabbas, washes his hands, and hands Jesus over for scourging and crucifixion. Soldiers mock Jesus; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; Jesus is crucified at Golgotha with two thieves amid darkness and temple signs. Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus, and the tomb is sealed and guarded.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Mary Magdalene and the other Mary visiting Jesus’ tomb, an earthquake, an angel rolling away the stone, and the guards’ fear. The angel announces Jesus is risen and sends the women to tell the disciples; Jesus appears to them and directs them to Galilee. The chief priests bribe soldiers to report the body was stolen. Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain, declares his authority, and commissions them to teach, baptize, and observe his commandments.

This chapter contains 45 verses and records John the Baptist preaching repentance and baptizing in the Jordan, foretelling one greater. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends, and a heavenly voice speaks; Jesus is tempted in the wilderness. After John’s imprisonment Jesus preaches in Galilee, calls Simon, Andrew, James, and John, teaches in Capernaum, casts out an unclean spirit, heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others, prays alone, preaches through Galilee, and cleanses a leper.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Jesus in Capernaum forgiving and healing a paralytic lowered through a roof, amid scribes’ objections. It covers Jesus calling Levi and dining with tax collectors and sinners, answering criticism. It includes questions about fasting with parables of new cloth and new wine. It describes a Sabbath dispute over plucking grain, citing David and declaring the Son of man Lord of the Sabbath.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jesus healing a man’s withered hand in a synagogue on the sabbath, prompting Pharisees and Herodians to plot against him. It describes crowds from many regions seeking healing, unclean spirits calling him Son of God, and Jesus commanding silence. Jesus appoints the twelve apostles by name. His family seeks to restrain him, scribes accuse him of using Beelzebub, and he answers with sayings on division, binding the strong man, forgiveness and blasphemy against the Holy Ghost, and true kin as doers of God’s will.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Jesus teaching by the sea from a boat, giving parables including the sower and its explanation, the lamp on a stand, measuring what one hears, seed growing secretly, and the mustard seed. It notes he explains privately to his disciples. It ends with Jesus crossing the sea, calming a windstorm, and questioning the disciples’ fear and lack of faith.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Jesus crossing to the Gadarenes, casting unclean spirits (“Legion”) from a tomb-dwelling man into about two thousand swine, and being asked to depart; the healed man proclaims in Decapolis. Back across the sea, Jairus seeks healing for his dying daughter. A woman with a twelve-year issue of blood touches Jesus’ garment and is healed. Jesus raises Jairus’s twelve-year-old daughter and instructs secrecy and food.

This chapter contains 56 verses and records Jesus teaching in his hometown synagogue and being rejected, healing a few, and traveling to teach. Jesus sends the twelve out in pairs with instructions, and they preach repentance, cast out demons, and heal. Herod hears of Jesus and the chapter recounts John the Baptist’s imprisonment and beheading. Jesus feeds five thousand, walks on the sea, reaches Gennesaret, and heals many who touch him.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Pharisees and scribes criticizing the disciples’ eating with unwashed hands; Jesus cites Isaiah, contrasts God’s commandments with human traditions, and teaches that defilement comes from within, listing sins from the heart. Jesus goes to Tyre and Sidon and delivers a Syrophoenician woman’s daughter from an unclean spirit. He then travels through Decapolis, heals a deaf man with a speech impediment, and orders silence though the miracle is widely reported.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jesus feeding about four thousand with seven loaves and a few fish, then traveling to Dalmanutha and refusing Pharisees’ request for a sign. Jesus warns about the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod. In Bethsaida he heals a blind man in two stages. Near Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ; Jesus predicts suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection, rebukes Peter, and teaches self-denial, taking up the cross, and not being ashamed of him.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records Jesus’ transfiguration before Peter, James, and John, with Moses and Elijah and a voice from a cloud, and his command to keep silence until his resurrection. Jesus explains Elijah’s coming and predicts his suffering and rising. He casts out a dumb and deaf spirit, teaches prayer and fasting, and instructs on humility, receiving children, not forbidding others, rewards, avoiding offenses, warnings of hell, and salt and peace.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records Jesus teaching in Judea beyond the Jordan on divorce and adultery, blessing little children, and instructing a rich man to sell possessions and follow him. He teaches about riches and the kingdom, promises recompense for those who leave all, foretells his death and resurrection, corrects James and John on greatness and service, and heals blind Bartimaeus near Jericho.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Jesus sending disciples to obtain a colt near Bethphage and Bethany, his entry into Jerusalem with crowds spreading garments and branches, and his visit to the temple. It covers Jesus cursing a fig tree, cleansing the temple of merchants and moneychangers, and teaching about prayer, faith, and forgiving others. Chief priests, scribes, and elders question his authority; he counters with John’s baptism and gives no answer.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Jesus teaching the parable of the vineyard and rejected son, prompting leaders to seek his arrest. Pharisees and Herodians question tribute to Caesar; Jesus answers to render to Caesar and to God. Sadducees test resurrection with levirate marriage; Jesus explains no marriage in resurrection and cites Moses. A scribe asks the greatest commandment. Jesus questions David’s son, warns against scribes, and commends a poor widow’s offering.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Jesus predicting the temple’s destruction and answering Peter, James, John, and Andrew on the Mount of Olives. He warns against deceivers, wars, earthquakes, famines, persecution, and family betrayal, and says the gospel is preached to all nations. He instructs flight from Judea at the abomination of desolation, describes tribulation and cosmic signs, the Son of man’s coming and gathering the elect, and commands watchfulness since the time is unknown.

This chapter contains 72 verses and records priests and scribes plotting to kill Jesus, a woman anointing him in Bethany, and Judas arranging betrayal. Jesus directs Passover preparations, predicts a betrayer, and institutes bread and cup at the meal. He foretells disciples’ scattering and Peter’s denial, prays in Gethsemane, and is arrested. Jesus is tried before the high priest and council, condemned, mocked, and beaten. Peter denies Jesus three times before the cock crows twice and weeps.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Jesus being delivered by the council to Pilate, questioned as King of the Jews, and accused while remaining mostly silent. Pilate releases Barabbas, scourges Jesus, and hands him to be crucified. Soldiers mock him; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross. Jesus is crucified at Golgotha with two thieves; darkness falls; he dies; the temple veil tears. A centurion comments; women watch. Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus; Marys note the tomb.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records women visiting Jesus’ tomb with spices, finding the stone rolled away, and hearing a young man announce Jesus is risen and will meet the disciples in Galilee. Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and to two disciples, and the others initially do not believe. He appears to the eleven, rebukes unbelief, commands preaching and baptism, lists accompanying signs, ascends to heaven, and the disciples preach with confirming signs.

This chapter contains 80 verses and records Luke’s purpose for writing to Theophilus, Gabriel’s announcement to Zacharias of John’s birth and Zacharias’s muteness, and Elisabeth’s conception. Gabriel announces to Mary in Nazareth that she will bear Jesus. Mary visits Elisabeth; Elisabeth speaks by the Spirit and Mary gives a hymn. John is born, circumcised, and named; Zacharias speaks again and prophesies. John grows and lives in the deserts.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records Caesar Augustus’s taxing that brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger. Angels announce the birth to shepherds, who visit and report it. Jesus is circumcised and named, then presented in Jerusalem with sacrifices; Simeon and Anna speak about him. The family returns to Nazareth. At age twelve Jesus remains in the temple, then returns home and grows.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records John the Baptist’s ministry near the Jordan under Tiberius, Pilate, Herod, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. John preaches baptism of repentance, warns crowds, and gives ethical instructions to people, tax collectors, and soldiers. He foretells one mightier who baptizes with the Holy Ghost and fire; Herod imprisons John. Jesus is baptized; heaven opens, the Spirit descends, and a voice speaks. A genealogy traces Jesus from Joseph back to Adam.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Jesus’ forty-day temptation in the wilderness and his Scripture responses. It covers his return to Galilee, teaching in synagogues, and reading Isaiah in Nazareth, declaring its fulfillment, and being rejected and threatened. It describes ministry in Capernaum: casting out an unclean spirit, healing Simon’s mother-in-law and many sick, silencing demons, withdrawing to a desert place, and continuing to preach in Galilee.

This chapter contains 39 verses and records Jesus teaching from Simon’s boat at the lake of Gennesaret, the miraculous catch of fish, and the call of Simon Peter, James, and John. It covers Jesus cleansing a leper and instructing him to show himself to the priest. It records healing a paralytic lowered through a roof and declaring sins forgiven. It includes Levi’s call and feast, disputes about sinners and fasting, and parables of new cloth and new wine.

This chapter contains 49 verses and records Sabbath disputes over disciples plucking grain and Jesus healing a man with a withered hand, asserting authority over the Sabbath. Jesus prays on a mountain, chooses twelve apostles, and heals crowds from Judea, Jerusalem, Tyre, and Sidon. It covers blessings and woes, commands to love enemies, give, forgive, and avoid judging, plus parables on blind guides, specks and beams, trees and fruit, and building on rock versus sand.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records Jesus healing a centurion’s servant in Capernaum, raising a widow’s only son at Nain, and John the Baptist sending disciples to ask Jesus’ identity; Jesus points to his miracles and preaching and speaks about John and responses to his baptism. It includes a meal at Simon the Pharisee’s house where a sinful woman anoints Jesus’ feet; Jesus gives a two-debtors parable, declares her sins forgiven, and sends her in peace.

This chapter contains 56 verses and records Jesus preaching the kingdom through cities with the twelve and supported by women including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna. It gives the parable of the sower with its explanation, teachings on a lamp and hearing, and defines his family as doers of God’s word. Jesus calms a storm, casts “Legion” into swine in Gadara, heals a hemorrhaging woman, and raises Jairus’s daughter.

This chapter contains 62 verses and records Jesus sending the twelve to preach and heal with authority, Herod’s questions, and the feeding of about five thousand near Bethsaida. It covers Peter’s confession, Jesus foretelling suffering, death, and resurrection, and teaching self-denial. It records the transfiguration with Moses and Elijah, healing a demon-possessed boy, teaching humility and tolerance, travel toward Jerusalem, Samaritan rejection, and sayings on discipleship costs.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Jesus appointing and sending seventy disciples with instructions on hospitality, healing, and proclaiming God’s kingdom, and warnings to unreceptive cities (Chorazin, Bethsaida, Capernaum). The seventy return reporting authority over demons; Jesus speaks of Satan’s fall and rejoicing in heaven. He answers a lawyer with the Good Samaritan parable, and visits Martha and Mary, commending Mary’s choice.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records Jesus teaching prayer (the Lord’s Prayer), urging persistence in asking, seeking, and knocking, and promising the Holy Spirit to those who ask. He casts out a mute demon, answers accusations of using Beelzebub, warns about an unclean spirit’s return, and rebukes sign-seekers with Jonah, Nineveh, and the queen of the south. He teaches about light and the eye, pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers, and opponents seek to accuse him.

This chapter contains 59 verses and records Jesus warning disciples against Pharisaic hypocrisy, urging fear of God, confession of him, and reliance on the Holy Ghost in trials. He refuses to arbitrate an inheritance dispute, warns against covetousness, and gives the parable of the rich fool. He teaches not to worry, to seek God’s kingdom, give alms, and be watchful like servants. He speaks of accountability, coming division, discerning the times, and reconciling with an adversary before judgment.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jesus teaching that disasters do not prove greater guilt and calling all to repent; he gives the parable of the barren fig tree. In a synagogue on the sabbath he heals a woman bowed eighteen years and answers the ruler. He compares God’s kingdom to mustard seed and leaven, teaches about the narrow gate and exclusion, notes people from all directions entering. Pharisees warn of Herod; Jesus speaks of his mission and laments Jerusalem’s rejection.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Jesus dining at a chief Pharisee’s house on the Sabbath, healing a man with dropsy, and disputing Sabbath healing. He teaches a parable on taking the lowest seat and instructs hosts to invite the poor, maimed, lame, and blind. He gives the parable of the great supper with refused invitations and new guests gathered. He states conditions of discipleship, counting the cost, forsaking all, and warns about salt losing savor.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Jesus teaching parables after Pharisees and scribes complain that he receives sinners. It includes the lost sheep sought by its owner, the lost coin found by a woman, and the prodigal son who wastes his inheritance, returns, and is received by his father. The elder son objects, and the father explains rejoicing over the restored son.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Jesus’ parable of the unjust steward and teachings on faithful stewardship, using wealth, and the impossibility of serving both God and mammon. Pharisees mock him; he rebukes their self-justification, mentions the law and prophets until John, affirms the law’s permanence, and states divorce and remarriage as adultery. It also records the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, their deaths, Abraham’s bosom, torment, and warning to heed Moses and the prophets.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Jesus warning against causing offenses, commanding repeated forgiveness, and teaching about faith and duty. While traveling toward Jerusalem through Samaria and Galilee, he heals ten lepers; one Samaritan returns to give thanks. Jesus answers Pharisees about the kingdom of God and teaches disciples about the Son of man’s coming, comparing it to Noah and Lot, urging readiness, and describing people taken and left.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Jesus’ parables of the persistent widow and the unjust judge, and the Pharisee and the publican praying in the temple. It describes Jesus blessing infants and teaching about receiving God’s kingdom like a child. A ruler asks about eternal life; Jesus cites commandments and tells him to sell possessions and follow him, teaching on riches and salvation. Jesus predicts his suffering, death, and resurrection, then heals a blind beggar near Jericho.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Jesus meeting Zacchaeus in Jericho and staying at his house as Zacchaeus vows restitution. Jesus gives the parable of the nobleman and the ten pounds, rewarding faithful servants and judging the unfaithful and enemies. Near Jerusalem he procures a colt, enters from the Mount of Olives amid disciples’ praise, weeps over Jerusalem, foretells its siege and destruction, cleanses the temple, and teaches while leaders seek to kill him.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Jesus teaching in the temple, being questioned about his authority, and countering with a question about John’s baptism. He gives the parable of the vineyard and rejected stone. Spies ask about paying tribute to Caesar; Jesus answers to render to Caesar and to God. Sadducees question resurrection; Jesus affirms resurrection from Moses. He questions David calling the Christ “Lord” and warns against scribes’ hypocrisy and exploitation.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jesus observing the widow’s two mites and comparing her gift to the rich. He foretells the temple’s destruction and gives signs of coming deception, wars, disasters, and persecution. He predicts Jerusalem surrounded, desolated, and its people slain or captive. He describes cosmic signs and the Son of man’s coming, gives the fig tree parable, and commands watchfulness and prayer while teaching in the temple and lodging on the Mount of Olives.

This chapter contains 71 verses and records Passover approaching, chief priests plotting, and Judas agreeing to betray Jesus for money. Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover, institutes bread and cup in remembrance, and teaches humility and service. He warns Peter of denial and speaks of coming trials. On the Mount of Olives he prays, is strengthened by an angel, and is arrested; he heals a servant’s ear. Peter denies Jesus three times; Jesus is mocked, examined by the council, and questioned about being the Christ and Son of God.

This chapter contains 56 verses and records Jesus being led to Pilate, questioned, and sent to Herod, then returned; Pilate finds no fault yet releases Barabbas and sentences Jesus to crucifixion. Simon of Cyrene bears the cross; Jesus speaks to Jerusalem’s women. At Calvary Jesus is crucified with two criminals, prays for forgiveness, is mocked, and promises paradise to the repentant man. Darkness occurs; the temple veil tears; Jesus dies. A centurion testifies; Joseph of Arimathaea buries Jesus; women prepare spices and rest on the Sabbath.

This chapter contains 53 verses and records women finding Jesus’ empty tomb, two angels announcing his resurrection, and the report to the apostles; Peter visits the sepulchre. Jesus appears to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, explains scriptures, is recognized in breaking bread, and vanishes. He appears to the gathered disciples, shows his hands and feet, eats food, commissions preaching repentance and remission of sins, promises power from on high, and ascends near Bethany.

This chapter contains 51 verses and records the Word’s preexistence with God, creation, life and light, and the Word becoming flesh as Jesus Christ. It describes John the Baptist’s witness, his denial of being the Christ, and his baptizing at Bethabara beyond Jordan. John identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God and Son of God. Jesus calls Andrew, Simon Peter (Cephas), Philip, and Nathanael, who confesses Jesus as King of Israel.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jesus turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana, leading his disciples to believe. It notes his brief stay in Capernaum with his mother, brethren, and disciples. At Passover in Jerusalem, he drives merchants and money changers from the temple and is questioned for a sign. He speaks of raising “the temple” in three days, referring to his body. Many believe due to miracles, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, knowing people’s hearts.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Nicodemus, a Pharisee ruler, visiting Jesus at night and hearing about being born again, born of water and the Spirit, and the Son of man being lifted up for eternal life through belief. It contrasts light and darkness and condemnation. Jesus and his disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes at Aenon near Salim; John affirms he is not the Christ and says Jesus must increase. It concludes with testimony about the Son’s authority and consequences of belief or unbelief.

This chapter contains 54 verses and records Jesus leaving Judea for Galilee through Samaria, speaking with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well in Sychar about living water, worship, and his identity as the Christ. The woman testifies, and many Samaritans believe; Jesus stays two days. In Galilee he returns to Cana and heals a nobleman’s son in Capernaum by word.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Jesus healing a man infirm for 38 years at the pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem on the sabbath, leading to Jewish opposition. Jesus speaks of working as the Father works, his authority to give life, raise the dead, and execute judgment. He cites witnesses to his mission: John the Baptist, his works, the Father, the Scriptures, and Moses.

This chapter contains 71 verses and records Jesus crossing the Sea of Galilee, feeding about five thousand with five barley loaves and two fishes, and gathering twelve baskets of fragments. The crowd seeks to make him king, and he withdraws. He later walks on the sea to the disciples’ boat and reaches Capernaum. In Capernaum’s synagogue he teaches about the bread of life, belief, and eternal life; many disciples depart, Peter affirms loyalty, and Jesus identifies Judas as a betrayer.

This chapter contains 53 verses and records Jesus staying in Galilee because Jews seek to kill him, then going secretly to Jerusalem for the Feast of Tabernacles. He teaches in the temple about his doctrine, Moses’ law, circumcision, and judging righteously, and defends healing on the sabbath. Authorities attempt arrest; people debate his identity. Jesus invites the thirsty to come and promises living water, speaking of the Spirit. Officers return empty-handed; Nicodemus cites due process.

This chapter contains 59 verses and records Jesus teaching in the temple after going from the mount of Olives, responding to scribes and Pharisees who bring an adulterous woman, and dismissing her accusers while telling her to sin no more. It covers Jesus declaring himself the light of the world, disputing with Pharisees about witness and the Father, warning of dying in sins, teaching about truth and freedom from sin, confronting claims of Abrahamic descent, and stating “Before Abraham was, I am,” after which they attempt to stone him.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Jesus healing a man blind from birth by making clay, anointing his eyes, and sending him to wash in the pool of Siloam on the Sabbath. Neighbors and Pharisees question the man and his parents; Pharisees dispute Jesus’ authority and expel the healed man. Jesus later identifies himself as the Son of God, and the man believes. Jesus speaks of spiritual sight and blindness to Pharisees.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Jesus teaching the sheepfold parable, identifying himself as the door and the good shepherd who lays down his life and knows his sheep, contrasting thieves and hirelings, and mentioning “other sheep.” It notes division among the Jews. At the feast of dedication in Jerusalem, Jesus speaks in Solomon’s porch about belief, eternal life, and unity with the Father; opponents accuse blasphemy and attempt stoning and arrest. Jesus withdraws beyond Jordan, where many believe.

This chapter contains 57 verses and records Lazarus of Bethany becoming sick and dying, Jesus delaying, then traveling to Judea. Jesus meets Martha and Mary, speaks of resurrection and belief, weeps, and raises Lazarus from a cave tomb after four days. Many believe; others report to Pharisees. Chief priests and Pharisees, led by Caiaphas, plan Jesus’ death. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim as Passover approaches and leaders order his capture.

This chapter contains 50 verses and records Jesus in Bethany where Mary anoints his feet and Judas objects; chief priests plan to kill Lazarus. It covers Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem with palm branches, Greeks seeking him, and teachings on his coming death, serving him, and being the light. A heavenly voice speaks; Jesus explains judgment and belief, notes unbelief fulfilling Isaiah, and affirms speaking the Father’s commandment.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Jesus washing the disciples’ feet at supper before Passover, teaching them to serve one another and noting that not all are clean. Jesus predicts betrayal, identifies Judas by giving him a dipped sop, and Judas leaves. Jesus speaks of his coming departure and glorification, gives a new commandment to love one another, and foretells Peter’s threefold denial.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Jesus consoling his disciples, promising to prepare a place in the Father’s house and to return. He answers Thomas about the way to the Father, teaches Philip about seeing the Father through him, and promises believers will do works and have prayers answered in his name. He commands keeping his commandments, promises the Comforter/Holy Ghost, gives peace, foretells his departure, and mentions the prince of this world.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Jesus teaching that he is the true vine and disciples must abide in him to bear fruit, with unfruitful branches removed. He commands keeping his commandments and loving one another, calls disciples friends, and says he chooses and ordains them to bear lasting fruit and pray in his name. He warns of the world’s hatred and persecution, explains responsibility for rejecting his words and works, cites “hated without a cause,” and promises the Comforter to testify; disciples also witness.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Jesus warning the disciples of expulsion from synagogues and persecution, explaining his departure to the Father, and promising the Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who convicts the world and guides into truth. Jesus speaks of a short time of sorrow turning to joy, instructs prayer to the Father in his name, affirms his origin and return to the Father, predicts the disciples’ scattering, and promises peace amid tribulation.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Jesus praying to the Father to glorify him, affirming authority to give eternal life and defining it as knowing the true God and Jesus Christ. He prays for the disciples, not the world, asking their protection, joy, sanctification by truth, and unity. He notes one lost “son of perdition,” sends them into the world, and prays also for future believers to be one and share his glory and love.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Jesus crossing the brook Cedron to a garden, Judas leading officers to arrest him, and Peter cutting off Malchus’s ear before Jesus is bound and taken to Annas and then Caiaphas. Peter enters the courtyard and denies Jesus three times as the cock crows. Jesus is questioned about his teaching and struck. Jesus is brought to Pilate, speaks of his kingship and truth, and Pilate finds no fault; the crowd chooses Barabbas for release.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Pilate scourging Jesus, soldiers mocking him with a crown of thorns, and leaders demanding crucifixion. Pilate sentences Jesus at Gabbatha. Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two others with an inscription in three languages. Soldiers divide his garments by lot. Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, receives vinegar, and dies. His legs are not broken; his side is pierced. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him in a nearby new tomb.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Mary Magdalene finding the stone removed and reporting to Peter and the other disciple, who inspect the empty tomb and linen cloths. Mary sees two angels and then Jesus, who tells her to report to the disciples. Jesus appears to the disciples, shows his wounds, commissions them, gives the Holy Ghost, and speaks of remitting or retaining sins. Thomas doubts, then sees Jesus and confesses him. The chapter states the purpose of the written signs.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jesus appearing to disciples at the Sea of Tiberias, directing a catch of 153 fish and eating with them. Jesus questions Peter three times about love and commands him to feed his lambs/sheep, then foretells Peter’s death and tells him to follow. Peter asks about the beloved disciple; Jesus answers and a rumor is corrected. The author affirms testimony and notes many unrecorded deeds.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances and teaching for forty days, his command to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Ghost, and his ascension from the Mount of Olives. Two men in white speak of his return. The apostles and others pray together in Jerusalem. Peter addresses about 120 disciples about Judas’ death and the “field of blood,” cites Psalms, and Matthias is chosen by lot to replace Judas.

This chapter contains 47 verses and records Pentecost in Jerusalem, when the apostles receive the Holy Ghost with wind and tongues like fire and speak in other languages heard by Jews from many regions. Peter addresses the crowd, cites Joel and David, proclaims Jesus’ crucifixion, resurrection, and exaltation, and calls for repentance and baptism. About three thousand are baptized; believers continue in teaching, fellowship, prayers, signs, shared goods, temple worship, and house-to-house breaking of bread.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Peter and John healing a man lame from birth at the temple gate called Beautiful, causing public amazement in Solomon’s porch. Peter attributes the miracle to faith in Jesus Christ, recounts Israel’s rejection of Jesus before Pilate, and testifies of Jesus’ resurrection. He calls for repentance, cites Moses and the prophets, references the Abrahamic covenant, and states that Jesus is sent first to bless Israel by turning people from iniquities.

This chapter contains 37 verses and records Peter and John arrested in Jerusalem and questioned by rulers including Annas and Caiaphas about healing a man. Peter attributes the act to Jesus Christ’s name and proclaims salvation through him; the council threatens them and releases them. The believers pray for boldness; the place shakes and they speak God’s word. The church shares possessions, distributes to needs, and Barnabas sells land and gives the money.

This chapter contains 42 verses and records Ananias and Sapphira selling land, withholding part of the price, being confronted by Peter for lying, and dying, causing fear in the church. It covers apostles doing signs and healings in Jerusalem, including Peter’s shadow. The Sadducees imprison the apostles; an angel frees them to teach in the temple. They appear before the council; Peter testifies of Jesus. Gamaliel advises restraint; the apostles are beaten, warned, and continue preaching daily.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records a dispute over neglected Grecian widows, leading the Twelve to appoint seven men—Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas—to oversee daily ministration while the apostles devote themselves to prayer and the word. It notes growth of disciples in Jerusalem and priests believing. Stephen performs wonders, debates synagogues, is accused of blasphemy, arrested, and brought before the council.

This chapter contains 60 verses and records Stephen’s defense before the high priest, recounting Israel’s history from Abraham through Joseph and Moses, the exodus, wilderness rebellion, idolatry, and the tabernacle and temple. Stephen accuses the council of resisting the Holy Spirit and killing the prophets and the Just One. He sees Jesus at God’s right hand and is stoned outside the city; witnesses place garments at Saul’s feet.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records persecution after Stephen’s death, with believers scattered from Jerusalem while Saul imprisons many. Philip preaches in Samaria, performs healings and exorcisms, and many are baptized, including Simon the sorcerer. Peter and John confer the Holy Ghost by laying on hands; Simon is rebuked for offering money. Philip later baptizes an Ethiopian eunuch on the Gaza road and then preaches from Azotus to Caesarea.

This chapter contains 43 verses and records Saul obtaining letters to arrest disciples in Damascus, encountering a heavenly light and Jesus, becoming blind, and being healed and baptized through Ananias. Saul preaches in Damascus, escapes a plot, and is accepted in Jerusalem through Barnabas before being sent to Tarsus. It also covers church growth, Peter healing Aeneas in Lydda, raising Tabitha in Joppa, and staying with Simon the tanner.

This chapter contains 48 verses and records Cornelius in Caesarea receiving an angelic vision to send for Peter in Joppa. Peter sees a sheet vision about clean and unclean animals and is told to go with Cornelius’s men. Peter visits Cornelius’s household, refuses worship, and explains not calling any person unclean. He preaches Jesus’ ministry, death, resurrection, and commanded witness. The Holy Ghost falls on Gentile hearers; Peter orders their baptism.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Peter defending his visit with uncircumcised Gentiles by recounting the Joppa vision, the Spirit’s command, Cornelius’s message from an angel, and the Holy Ghost falling on Gentiles; Jerusalem believers accept Gentile repentance. It covers scattered disciples preaching in Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, Barnabas and Saul teaching a year, disciples first called Christians, Agabus predicting famine, and Antioch sending relief to Judea.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Herod’s persecution of the church, including the killing of James and the imprisonment of Peter during unleavened bread. The church prays; an angel frees Peter, who goes to Mary’s house where Rhoda answers, reports to James and the brethren, and departs. Herod executes the guards and goes to Caesarea, addresses Tyre and Sidon, is struck by an angel and dies. The word grows; Barnabas and Saul return with John Mark.

This chapter contains 52 verses and records prophets and teachers at Antioch sending Barnabas and Saul by the Holy Ghost; they travel through Seleucia, Cyprus, and preach in synagogues. In Paphos Paul blinds Elymas and Sergius Paulus believes. They go to Perga as John returns to Jerusalem, then to Pisidian Antioch where Paul recounts Israel’s history and proclaims Jesus’ death and resurrection, forgiveness and justification. Jews oppose, Gentiles believe, persecution expels them to Iconium.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Paul and Barnabas preaching in Iconium amid division and threats, fleeing to Lystra and Derbe. Paul heals a cripple in Lystra; the crowd calls them Jupiter and Mercurius and attempts sacrifice, which they refuse while urging worship of the living God. Jews incite a stoning of Paul. They preach in Derbe, revisit cities to strengthen disciples, appoint elders with fasting, travel through Pisidia, Pamphylia, Perga, and Attalia, and report in Antioch.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records a dispute over requiring Gentile circumcision and keeping Moses’ law, leading Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem. Apostles and elders hear testimony from Peter, Paul, and Barnabas; James proposes Gentiles avoid idolatry, fornication, blood, and strangled things. A letter is sent with Judas Barsabas and Silas to Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. Paul and Barnabas later separate over John Mark; Barnabas goes to Cyprus, Paul travels with Silas confirming churches.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Paul recruiting Timothy at Derbe and Lystra, circumcising him, and delivering Jerusalem decrees as churches grow. The Spirit prevents preaching in Asia and Bithynia; Paul sees a Macedonian vision and travels to Philippi. Lydia and her household are baptized. Paul casts out a divining spirit; Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, an earthquake opens doors, and the jailer’s household is baptized. Paul asserts Roman citizenship; magistrates release them, and they depart via Lydia’s house.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Paul and Silas preaching in Thessalonica, some believing, and opposition leading to Jason being accused and released on security. Paul and Silas go to Berea, where many examine Scripture and believe, but Thessalonian Jews stir trouble. Paul is sent to Athens, disputes in synagogue and marketplace, and speaks at the Areopagus about the Creator, repentance, and resurrection; some mock, others believe, including Dionysius and Damaris.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Paul’s ministry in Corinth with Aquila and Priscilla, his synagogue reasoning, and many Corinthians believing and being baptized, including Crispus. The Lord encourages Paul in a vision; he teaches 18 months. Jews accuse Paul before Gallio, who dismisses the case; Sosthenes is beaten. Paul departs via Cenchrea and Ephesus to Caesarea and Antioch, then strengthens Galatia and Phrygia. Apollos arrives in Ephesus, is instructed by Aquila and Priscilla, and powerfully argues in Achaia that Jesus is Christ.

This chapter contains 41 verses and records Paul’s ministry in Ephesus, where about twelve disciples baptized into John’s baptism are baptized in Jesus’ name and receive the Holy Ghost by laying on of hands. Paul teaches in the synagogue, then daily in Tyrannus’s school for two years; miracles occur and the sons of Sceva fail at exorcism. Converts confess and burn magic books. Demetrius incites a riot over Diana shrines; Gaius and Aristarchus are seized, and the townclerk dismisses the assembly.

This chapter contains 38 verses and records Paul’s travels from Ephesus through Macedonia and Greece, then back via Philippi to Troas, where he preaches and Eutychus falls and is restored alive. It lists companions and sailing stops to Miletus. From Miletus Paul summons Ephesian elders, recounts his ministry, warns of false teachers, charges them to shepherd the church, models self-support and giving, then prays and departs amid their farewell.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Paul’s travel by ship to Tyre, Ptolemais, and Caesarea, where disciples and Agabus warn of his binding in Jerusalem. Paul proceeds to Jerusalem, meets James and the elders, and joins four men in a purification vow at the temple. Jews from Asia accuse him of teaching against the law and bringing Greeks into the temple, causing a riot. The Roman chief captain arrests Paul, rescues him from violence, and permits him to address the crowd.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Paul’s defense to the Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew, recounting his Jewish upbringing under Gamaliel, his persecution of believers, and his Damascus road encounter with Jesus. He describes Ananias restoring his sight and urging baptism, and a temple vision directing him to the Gentiles. The crowd riots; a Roman commander orders scourging, but Paul claims Roman citizenship. The commander releases him and convenes the council.

This chapter contains 35 verses and records Paul before the Sanhedrin, where Ananias orders him struck and Paul cites the resurrection, causing dispute between Pharisees and Sadducees. Roman soldiers remove Paul to the fortress, and the Lord tells him he must testify in Rome. Over forty Jews plot to kill Paul, but his nephew warns the tribune Claudius Lysias. Lysias sends Paul under heavy escort to Caesarea with a letter to Governor Felix, who orders Paul kept in Herod’s judgment hall pending accusers.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Paul’s hearing before Governor Felix. Ananias, elders, and Tertullus accuse Paul of sedition, leading the Nazarenes, and profaning the temple. Paul denies stirring crowds, affirms worship according to the Law and Prophets, and states his belief in the resurrection. Felix postpones judgment, orders Paul kept with limited liberty, hears him with Drusilla, seeks a bribe, and leaves Paul bound until Festus succeeds him.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Festus arriving in the province, hearing Jewish leaders’ accusations against Paul, and keeping Paul in Caesarea despite a plot to kill him. Paul denies offenses and appeals to Caesar, so Festus orders him sent. Agrippa and Bernice visit; Festus explains the case, noting disputes about Jesus’ resurrection, and presents Paul to Agrippa to determine charges to report.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Paul’s defense before King Agrippa, with Festus and Bernice present. Paul recounts his Pharisaic life, persecution of believers, and his Damascus road encounter with Jesus, receiving a commission to witness to Jews and Gentiles. He states he preaches repentance and fulfillment of Moses and the prophets, including Christ’s suffering and resurrection. Festus challenges him; Agrippa responds. They conclude Paul is not guilty but is bound by his appeal to Caesar.

This chapter contains 44 verses and records Paul’s voyage as a prisoner toward Italy under Centurion Julius. The party sails from Sidon past Cyprus to Myra, changes to an Alexandrian ship, and reaches Fair Havens in Crete. Ignoring Paul’s warning, they depart and face the storm Euroclydon, jettison cargo, and drift fourteen nights. Paul reports an angel’s assurance of survival and a shipwreck on an island. Soldiers prevent escape, and all 276 reach land safely.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Paul and the shipwrecked company arriving on Melita, receiving help, and Paul surviving a viper bite and healing Publius’s father and other sick people. After three months they sail via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli to Rome, where believers meet them. Paul lives under guard, meets Jewish leaders, explains his appeal to Caesar, teaches about Jesus from Moses and the prophets, sees mixed response, cites Isaiah, and preaches two years in a rented house.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Paul’s greeting to believers in Rome, identifying his apostleship and the gospel concerning Jesus Christ descended from David and raised from the dead. Paul thanks God for their faith, states his desire to visit and preach, and declares the gospel brings salvation to Jew and Greek. It describes God’s wrath against idolatry and unrighteousness, people being given over to uncleanness and reprobate minds, and lists various sins and their judgment.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Paul’s warning against judging others while committing the same sins, affirming God’s impartial judgment according to deeds, and calling people to repentance. It states that Gentiles without the law and Jews under the law are judged by their actions, not merely hearing. It addresses Jews who boast in the law yet break it, discusses circumcision’s value only with obedience, and distinguishes inward Jewish identity and heart circumcision from outward rites.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Paul discussing Jewish advantage through receiving God’s oracles, denying that human unbelief nullifies God’s truth, and rejecting doing evil for good results. It states Jews and Gentiles are all under sin, citing Scripture on universal unrighteousness. It says the law brings knowledge of sin, not justification. It presents righteousness through faith in Jesus Christ, justification by grace through Christ’s redemption, exclusion of boasting, one God justifying Jews and Gentiles by faith, and faith establishing the law.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Paul’s argument that Abraham is counted righteous by faith, not by works, citing Scripture and David on forgiveness and non-imputation of sin. It states Abraham receives circumcision as a sign after being justified, making him father of believing circumcised and uncircumcised. The promise comes through faith and grace, not law. It describes Abraham’s trust despite age and Sarah’s barrenness, and applies this to belief in God who raises Jesus.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes justification by faith bringing peace with God through Jesus Christ, access to grace, and rejoicing in hope and tribulations that produce endurance, character, and hope through the Holy Ghost. It records Christ dying for the ungodly, reconciliation by his death, and salvation by his life. It compares Adam’s sin and death with Christ’s gift of grace, justification, and eternal life.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Paul teaching that believers, baptized into Jesus Christ’s death, are to walk in newness of life and consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God. He commands not letting sin reign, not yielding members to unrighteousness, but yielding to God as instruments of righteousness. He contrasts servitude to sin leading to death with obedience leading to holiness and eternal life, concluding with wages of sin versus God’s gift through Christ.

This chapter contains 25 verses and describes Paul’s teaching that the law rules only while a person lives, using marriage to show release by death. It records believers becoming dead to the law through Christ to serve in newness of spirit. Paul explains the law reveals sin (including “Thou shalt not covet”) while sin uses the commandment to produce death. He recounts an inner conflict between delighting in God’s law and captivity to sin, concluding deliverance is through Jesus Christ.

This chapter contains 39 verses and describes freedom from condemnation for those in Christ who walk by the Spirit rather than the flesh. It contrasts fleshly and spiritual mindsets, teaches mortifying sinful deeds, and calls believers sons and heirs through adoption. It covers present sufferings, creation’s groaning, hope for bodily redemption, and the Spirit’s intercession. It states God’s foreknowledge, predestination, calling, justification, and glorification, and affirms no power separates believers from God’s love in Christ.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Paul’s sorrow for Israel and Israel’s privileges, including covenants, law, and Christ’s lineage. He distinguishes children of promise from physical descent, citing Isaac, Jacob and Esau, Moses, and Pharaoh to address God’s mercy and hardening. He uses potter-and-clay imagery, includes Gentile calling, a saved remnant of Israel, and faith versus works, ending with the stumbling stone in Zion.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul’s prayer for Israel’s salvation and his claim that Israel seeks its own righteousness rather than God’s. It states that Christ fulfills the law for believers and that salvation comes through believing in the risen Jesus and confessing him. It says Jew and Greek are alike in calling on the Lord, stresses preaching and hearing for faith, and cites Moses and Isaiah about Gentile reception and Israel’s disobedience.

This chapter contains 36 verses and records Paul stating God has not cast off Israel, citing Elijah and a remnant by grace, and describing Israel’s partial blindness and Gentile salvation. He warns Gentile believers not to boast, using an olive tree grafting metaphor and urging fear and perseverance. He states Israel can be grafted in again, cites prophecies of Israel’s salvation and covenant, notes God’s irrevocable calling, and concludes with praise of God’s wisdom.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul’s exhortations to present one’s body as a living sacrifice and be transformed by renewed minds. It describes humility and unity as one body with differing gifts such as prophecy, ministry, teaching, exhortation, giving, ruling, and mercy. It commands sincere love, diligence, prayer, hospitality, blessing persecutors, empathy, peace, honest conduct, and nonretaliation, including feeding enemies and overcoming evil with good.

This chapter contains 14 verses and covers submission to governing authorities as ordained by God, warning against resisting rulers, and commanding payment of taxes, customs, respect, and honor. It instructs believers to owe nothing except mutual love, citing commandments and stating love fulfills the law. It urges moral vigilance, casting off works of darkness, avoiding drunkenness and immorality, and putting on Jesus Christ.

This chapter contains 23 verses and covers receiving weaker believers without disputes, differing practices about eating foods and observing days, and forbidding despising or judging one another. It states all belong to the Lord and will stand before Christ’s judgment seat, giving account to God. It urges avoiding stumblingblocks, acting charitably, pursuing peace and edification, limiting food or wine if they offend, and acting from faith.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Paul’s exhortation for the strong to bear the weak, seek others’ edification, and receive one another in unity. It cites Scriptures about Christ’s service to Israel and Gentile praise and hope. Paul explains his Gentile ministry, signs, and preaching from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and his aim to evangelize new regions. He plans travel to Jerusalem, Rome, and Spain, mentions Macedonian and Achaian aid for Jerusalem, and requests prayer for safety and acceptance.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Paul commending Phebe of the church at Cenchrea and instructing the Romans to receive and assist her. He sends greetings to many believers and households in Rome, including Priscilla and Aquila and their house church, and relays greetings from his companions. He commands mutual greeting, warns against divisive deceivers, promises God will bruise Satan, and closes with a doxology about the revealed gospel.

This chapter contains 31 verses and records Paul and Sosthenes addressing the church at Corinth, giving thanks for their spiritual gifts and calling them to unity. Paul reports divisions (Paul, Apollos, Cephas, Christ) and notes he baptized only Crispus, Gaius, and Stephanas’s household. He contrasts human wisdom with preaching Christ crucified, citing Scripture, and states God chooses the weak to prevent boasting, urging glory in the Lord.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Paul telling the Corinthians he preaches Christ crucified without rhetorical wisdom, relying on the Spirit’s power so faith rests on God. He contrasts God’s hidden wisdom with worldly rulers’ ignorance, cites what God prepares for those who love him, and says the Spirit reveals God’s deep things. He distinguishes natural and spiritual discernment and states believers have the mind of Christ.

This chapter contains 23 verses and describes Paul addressing the Corinthians as carnal and divided over allegiance to Paul and Apollos. It explains ministers as servants, with God giving growth, and compares the church to God’s field and building. Paul lays the foundation of Jesus Christ and warns to build carefully, as works are tested by fire for reward or loss. It calls believers God’s temple, warns against defiling it, rejects worldly wisdom, forbids glorying in men, and affirms all things are theirs in Christ.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul urging the Corinthians to regard apostles as Christ’s servants and stewards who must be faithful, and to avoid judging before the Lord’s coming. He applies the lesson to himself and Apollos, warning against pride and boasting in gifts received. He contrasts the apostles’ hardships and humility with the Corinthians’ self-satisfaction, calls them to imitate him, sends Timothy, and plans a visit to test the “puffed up,” asking whether he should come with discipline or gentleness.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Paul addressing reported sexual immorality in the Corinthian church, specifically a man having his father’s wife. He rebukes their pride and instructs them, when assembled in Jesus’ name, to remove the offender and deliver him to Satan for destruction of the flesh. He uses leaven imagery to command purging wickedness, and directs believers not to associate or eat with professing brothers who practice specified sins, while distinguishing judgment inside the church from outsiders.

This chapter contains 20 verses and covers Paul’s rebuke of believers taking disputes to secular courts, urging judgment within the church and willingness to suffer wrong. It lists sins that exclude from inheriting the kingdom and notes believers are washed, sanctified, and justified. Paul warns that not all lawful things are beneficial, commands fleeing fornication, and teaches the body belongs to the Lord, is a member of Christ, a temple of the Holy Ghost, and must glorify God.

This chapter contains 40 verses and records Paul’s counsel on marriage, celibacy, and sexual duty. He addresses spouses’ mutual authority over their bodies, temporary abstinence for prayer, and marriage to avoid fornication. He gives commands about divorce and reconciliation, and guidance for believers married to unbelievers. He urges remaining in one’s calling (circumcision, slavery) and gives advice to virgins and widows amid present distress, stressing undistracted devotion to the Lord.

This chapter contains 13 verses and covers food offered to idols, contrasting knowledge and charity, affirming one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ. Paul notes some believers have weak consciences regarding idol sacrifices, and food does not commend anyone to God. He warns that exercising liberty can become a stumbling block, harming a weak brother and sinning against Christ, and vows to abstain if it causes offense.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records Paul defending his apostleship and stating his right to material support and marriage, citing Moses’ law and temple practice. He explains he renounces this right to avoid hindering the gospel, preaches from necessity, and makes the gospel without charge. He adapts to Jews, those under law, those without law, and the weak, and urges disciplined effort like athletes to avoid being disqualified.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Paul’s warning from Israel’s wilderness history (cloud, sea, manna, rock) against lust, idolatry, fornication, testing Christ, and murmuring. He urges vigilance in temptation, fleeing idolatry, and explains communion in Christ versus fellowship with demons. He gives guidance on eating meat sold or served, abstaining if identified as idol-sacrifice, and commands doing all to God’s glory without offending Jews, Gentiles, or the church.

This chapter contains 34 verses and records Paul urging imitation of him as he follows Christ, affirming the keeping of ordinances, and giving instructions on headship and head coverings while praying or prophesying, including comments on hair and church custom. He rebukes divisions and improper conduct at gatherings, recounts Jesus instituting the Lord’s Supper, warns against partaking unworthily, calls for self-examination, and directs believers to wait for one another and eat at home if hungry.

This chapter contains 31 verses and covers Paul’s instruction on spiritual gifts and their source in the same Spirit, Lord, and God. It lists gifts such as wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning spirits, tongues, and interpretation. It explains believers as one body in Christ, baptized by one Spirit across Jew/Gentile and bond/free, with diverse members needing each other. It names church roles (apostles, prophets, teachers, helps, governments) and urges seeking the best gifts.

This chapter contains 13 verses and covers Paul’s teaching that spiritual gifts, knowledge, faith, sacrifice, and martyrdom are worthless without charity. It lists charity’s qualities: patience, kindness, humility, selflessness, restraint, truthfulness, endurance, and hope. It contrasts charity’s permanence with the passing of prophecies, tongues, and knowledge, notes present partial understanding versus future completeness, and states faith, hope, and charity remain, with charity greatest.

This chapter contains 40 verses and covers Paul’s instructions to pursue love and prefer prophecy over tongues unless interpreted, because prophecy edifies the church. He explains praying and singing with understanding, and says tongues serve as a sign for unbelievers. He gives rules for orderly gatherings: limited tongue speakers with an interpreter, prophets speak in turn and others judge, and revelations yield priority. He commands women to keep silence, affirms his directives as the Lord’s commandments, and requires decency and order.

This chapter contains 58 verses and records Paul’s summary of the gospel: Christ dies, is buried, rises, and appears to Cephas, the Twelve, many brethren, James, the apostles, and Paul. It argues that denying resurrection makes faith and preaching vain, then outlines resurrection order and Christ’s reign until death is destroyed. It mentions baptism for the dead, warns against corrupting associations, explains resurrection bodies, and commands steadfast labor.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Paul’s instructions for a collection for the saints, weekly setting aside funds, and sending approved messengers to Jerusalem. It covers his travel plans through Macedonia, possible wintering in Corinth, and remaining at Ephesus until Pentecost. Paul gives directions about Timothy and Apollos, exhorts steadfastness and charity, commends Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, sends greetings, and adds a warning and closing benediction.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Paul and Timothy greeting the Corinthian church and saints in Achaia. Paul blesses God for comfort in tribulation and reports severe trouble in Asia, deliverance from death, and requests prayer and thanksgiving. He defends his sincere conduct and reliability, explains delayed travel plans to Corinth and Macedonia, affirms God’s promises in Christ, mentions God’s sealing and Spirit’s earnest, and says he delays to spare them, not to rule their faith.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Paul’s decision not to visit Corinth in sorrow, explaining his tearful letter and urging the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward a disciplined offender. He links mutual forgiveness to obedience and preventing Satan’s advantage. Paul recounts preaching at Troas, leaving for Macedonia due to missing Titus, and describes God’s triumph in Christ and sincere proclamation of God’s word.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s defense of his ministry without letters of commendation, calling the Corinthians Christ’s epistle written by the Spirit on hearts. He states God makes ministers of the new covenant, contrasting letter and Spirit. He compares Moses’ fading glory and veil with surpassing, lasting glory in Christ, describing removed veils, liberty in the Lord’s Spirit, and believers being transformed into the Lord’s image.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s perseverance in ministry, renouncing deceit and preaching Christ rather than self. It states the gospel is hidden from unbelievers whose minds are blinded, and God shines light in believers’ hearts. Paul describes apostles as fragile vessels enduring trouble and persecution while bearing Jesus’ death so his life is shown. He affirms resurrection hope, thanksgiving, inward renewal, and focusing on unseen eternal things over temporary visible afflictions.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul teaching about the earthly body and an eternal heavenly dwelling, walking by faith, and seeking acceptance by the Lord. It states all appear before Christ’s judgment seat. Paul explains his ministry motives and urges living for Christ who died and rose. It describes new creation in Christ, reconciliation through Christ, and believers as ambassadors of reconciliation.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul urging the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, declaring the present as the day of salvation. He lists hardships and virtues that commend God’s ministers and describes contrasting circumstances they endure. Paul appeals for mutual openness and enlarged hearts. He commands separation from unbelief and idolatry, affirming believers as God’s temple and promising divine reception as sons and daughters.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Paul urging believers to cleanse themselves and pursue holiness, defending his conduct toward the Corinthians. He describes troubles in Macedonia and comfort received through Titus’s arrival and report of their desire, mourning, and zeal. Paul explains his earlier letter caused temporary sorrow leading to repentance, contrasts godly and worldly sorrow, notes their renewed obedience, and expresses joy, comfort, and confidence in them.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Paul commending the Macedonian churches’ generosity despite affliction and poverty, urging the Corinthians to complete their promised collection for the saints. He cites Christ’s becoming poor, teaches giving according to what one has, and seeks fairness in supply. Paul sends Titus and two approved brothers to manage the gift transparently and requests public proof of love.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Paul’s instructions about the collection for the saints. He sends brethren ahead so Corinth is prepared and his boasting to Macedonia is not shamed. He urges giving freely and cheerfully, noting sowing bountifully leads to greater return and God supplies sufficiency. The gift meets saints’ needs, produces thanksgiving and glory to God, prompts prayers for the givers, and ends with thanks for God’s gift.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s appeal to the Corinthians with Christlike meekness while defending his authority. He contrasts spiritual warfare with carnal methods, describing weapons that overthrow strongholds and bring thoughts into obedience. Paul addresses criticism of his weak presence, warns he will act firmly if needed, rejects self-commendation, limits boasting to his God-given measure, plans wider gospel preaching, and states approval comes from the Lord.

This chapter contains 33 verses and records Paul urging the Corinthians to bear with his “folly,” warning against another Jesus, spirit, or gospel, and denouncing false apostles who disguise themselves. He explains preaching free of charge and being supported from Macedonia. Paul “boasts” of his Hebrew lineage and extensive sufferings, dangers, and care for churches, and recounts escaping arrest in Damascus under Aretas by being lowered in a basket.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul referencing visions and a man caught up to the third heaven and paradise, then describing a “thorn in the flesh” and the Lord’s reply that grace is sufficient and strength is perfected in weakness. He lists hardships borne for Christ, affirms apostolic signs among the Corinthians, plans a third visit without burdening them, addresses accusations of gain through Titus, and warns against unrepented sins and church conflicts.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Paul’s warning before a third visit to Corinth, citing the need for two or three witnesses and saying he will not spare persistent sinners. He answers demands for proof of Christ in him, urges self-examination in the faith, and prays they do no evil and pursue truth and perfection. He explains his authority is for edification, gives final exhortations to unity and peace, includes greetings, and ends with a benediction.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records Paul’s greeting to the churches of Galatia, affirming his apostleship by Jesus Christ and warning against turning to a different gospel, pronouncing a curse on any who preach another message. Paul states his gospel comes by revelation of Jesus Christ, recounts his former persecution of the church, his call to preach among the Gentiles, travels to Arabia and Damascus, later visits Peter and James in Jerusalem, then ministers in Syria and Cilicia.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul’s Jerusalem visit with Barnabas and Titus to present his gospel; Titus is not compelled to be circumcised despite false brethren. James, Cephas, and John recognize Paul’s mission to Gentiles and request remembering the poor. In Antioch Paul confronts Peter for withdrawing from Gentiles. Paul states justification is by faith in Jesus Christ, not works of the law, and affirms living unto God through Christ.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Paul rebuking the Galatians for turning from faith to works of the law, asking how they received the Spirit. He cites Abraham’s belief as righteousness, says those of faith are Abraham’s children, and notes justification is not by the law. He states Christ redeems from the law’s curse, explains the promise precedes the law, and describes the law as a temporary guardian until Christ. He affirms believers baptized into Christ are one and heirs of the promise.

This chapter contains 31 verses and covers heirs under guardians as a figure for bondage and adoption; God sends his Son to redeem those under the law and sends the Spirit, making believers sons and heirs. Paul warns against returning to observing times and seasons, recalls the Galatians’ former reception of him, and cautions about misleading zeal. He contrasts Abraham’s sons (Hagar and Sarah) as two covenants, Sinai and Jerusalem, and affirms believers as children of promise.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Paul urging believers to stand in Christ’s liberty and not seek justification by circumcision or the law. He teaches that faith works by love, warns against false persuasion, and commands serving one another and loving one’s neighbor. He contrasts walking in the Spirit with works of the flesh, lists each, states such sinners do not inherit God’s kingdom, lists the Spirit’s fruit, and warns against vainglory, provoking, and envy.

This chapter contains 18 verses and covers instructions to restore those caught in sin with meekness, bear one another’s burdens, test one’s own work, and support teachers. It states the principle of sowing and reaping, urges perseverance in doing good to all, and warns against those promoting circumcision to avoid persecution. Paul glories only in the cross, notes the new creature, pronounces peace on the Israel of God, mentions his bodily marks, and closes with a grace blessing.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Paul’s greeting to the saints at Ephesus, invoking grace and peace.
