It covers God’s blessings in Christ, election before the world, predestination to adoption, redemption and forgiveness through Christ’s blood, and the mystery of God’s will to unite all things in Christ. Believers hear the gospel, believe, and are sealed with the Holy Spirit. Paul prays for wisdom, hope, and knowledge of God’s power shown in Christ’s resurrection, exaltation, and headship over the church.

This chapter contains 22 verses and describes believers being made alive with Christ by grace through faith, not by works, and created for good works. It records Gentiles once alienated from Israel’s covenants being brought near by Christ’s blood. It covers Christ making Jews and Gentiles one, abolishing enmity, granting access to the Father by one Spirit, and forming the church as God’s household built on apostles, prophets, and Christ the cornerstone.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, explaining the revealed mystery that Gentiles are fellowheirs in Christ, his ministry to preach Christ among them, and God’s purpose made known through the church. He urges them not to faint at his tribulations, prays for spiritual strengthening, Christ dwelling in their hearts, and knowledge of Christ’s love, and ends with a doxology.

This chapter contains 32 verses and records Paul urging believers to walk worthy with humility, patience, love, and unity, affirming one body, Spirit, Lord, faith, baptism, and Father. It lists Christ’s gifts of ministries (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers) to build up the body to maturity. It commands putting off the old life and practicing truthfulness, controlled anger, honest labor, edifying speech, not grieving the Spirit, and replacing bitterness with kindness and forgiveness.

This chapter contains 33 verses and covers exhortations to imitate God and walk in love, avoiding sexual immorality, uncleanness, covetousness, corrupt speech, and deception. It contrasts darkness and light, urges wise living, redeeming time, understanding the Lord’s will, avoiding drunkenness, and being Spirit-filled with worship and thanksgiving. It commands mutual submission, wives’ submission to husbands, husbands’ love for wives, and compares marriage to Christ and the church.

This chapter contains 24 verses and covers instructions for children to obey parents and for fathers to nurture without provoking; servants to obey masters sincerely and masters to forbear threatening. It urges believers to be strong, put on the whole armor of God against spiritual powers, and pray continually. Paul requests prayer for bold gospel speech as an imprisoned ambassador, sends Tychicus with news, and closes with peace and grace.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Paul and Timothy greeting the saints at Philippi, including bishops and deacons, and giving thanks and prayer for their fellowship and growth in love and righteousness. Paul reports that his imprisonment advances the gospel, making believers bolder despite mixed motives in preaching. He expresses readiness for life or death, plans to remain for their progress, and commands steadfast unity, courage amid adversaries, and willingness to suffer for Christ.

This chapter contains 30 verses and records Paul’s call to unity, humility, and concern for others, urging believers to adopt Christ Jesus’ mindset: his self-emptying, servanthood, obedience to death on the cross, and God’s exaltation so every knee bows and every tongue confesses him Lord. Paul commands obedient conduct, working out salvation, avoiding grumbling, holding the word of life, and rejoicing. He plans to send Timothy and sends Epaphroditus, recently gravely ill, to be received with honor.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Paul urging rejoicing in the Lord and warning against evil workers who rely on fleshly circumcision. He lists his Jewish credentials and former persecution of the church, then counts such gains as loss to win Christ and receive righteousness by faith. He presses toward the goal, calls believers to follow his example, warns of enemies of the cross, and states believers’ citizenship is in heaven awaiting Christ’s transforming power.

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Paul urging the Philippians to stand fast, calling Euodias and Syntyche to unity, and asking a yokefellow to help them with Clement and other coworkers. He commands rejoicing, gentleness, prayer instead of anxiety, and right thinking and practice. Paul thanks them for financial support via Epaphroditus, notes contentment in all circumstances, promises God’s supply, and closes with greetings and a benediction.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records Paul and Timothy greeting the saints at Colosse, thanking God for their faith and love, and noting Epaphras’s ministry. Paul prays they gain knowledge, walk worthily, and give thanks for deliverance and redemption. It describes Christ’s supremacy in creation and the church and reconciliation through the cross. Paul urges continued faith, mentions his sufferings and stewardship, and proclaims the revealed mystery to Gentiles: “Christ in you.”

This chapter contains 23 verses and records Paul’s concern for believers in Colossae and Laodicea, urging unity, comfort, and steadfast faith in Christ. It warns against deceptive philosophy and human traditions. It states Christ’s fullness and headship, believers’ completeness, spiritual circumcision, baptism, forgiveness, and ordinances removed by the cross. It forbids judgment over food, festivals, or sabbaths, and rejects angel worship and ascetic rules.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records exhortations to seek things above with Christ, put to death sinful practices, and put off anger, malice, and lying while putting on the new person. It lists virtues such as mercy, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, love, peace, thankfulness, and worshipful teaching. It gives household commands for wives, husbands, children, fathers, and servants, urging wholehearted service to the Lord and impartial judgment for wrongdoing.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records instructions to masters to act justly, and exhortations to continue in prayer, seek open doors for preaching, walk wisely toward outsiders, and speak graciously. Paul sends Tychicus and Onesimus, relays greetings from Aristarchus, Mark, Justus, Epaphras, Luke, and Demas, instructs sharing the letter with Laodicea, urges Archippus to fulfill his ministry, and notes his bonds.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greeting the Thessalonian church with grace and peace, giving thanks and praying for their faith, love, and hope. It notes the gospel coming with power and assurance, and the believers receiving the word amid affliction with joy. The church becomes an example in Macedonia and Achaia, spreads the message, turns from idols to serve God, and waits for God’s Son from heaven, raised from the dead.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Paul’s defense of his ministry in Thessalonica: he preaches boldly after suffering at Philippi, speaks without deceit or flattery, and works to avoid burdening them. He describes gentle, parental care, exhorts them to walk worthy of God, and thanks God for their reception of the word. He notes their persecutions, his desire to revisit, Satan’s hindrance, and their joy at Christ’s coming.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records Paul being left alone at Athens and sending Timothy to Thessalonica to strengthen and encourage believers amid afflictions and predicted tribulation. Timothy returns with good news of their faith, love, and desire to see Paul, comforting him. Paul gives thanks, prays to visit and supply what is lacking, asks God to direct his way, and prays they abound in love and be established in holiness for Christ’s coming.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s exhortations that believers walk to please God, keep the commandments, and pursue sanctification by abstaining from fornication, avoiding defrauding others, and living in holiness. It addresses brotherly love, urging increase, quiet living, personal work, and honest conduct before outsiders. It explains hope for those who have died: the Lord’s coming, the dead in Christ rising first, and the living caught up to meet him, for mutual comfort.

This chapter contains 28 verses and covers the day of the Lord coming unexpectedly, urging believers to watch and be sober, equipped with faith, love, and hope. It calls them to comfort and edify one another, respect leaders, maintain peace, and practice patience and good toward all. It commands rejoicing, continual prayer, thanksgiving, not quenching the Spirit, valuing prophecy, testing all things, and avoiding evil, and closes with a sanctification prayer, greetings, and a charge to read the letter.

This chapter contains 12 verses and records Paul, Silvanus, and Timotheus greeting the Thessalonian church with grace and peace. It notes their growing faith, mutual charity, and endurance under persecutions, and says God repays affliction to their oppressors and gives rest at Jesus’ revelation with angels. It describes judgment on those rejecting the gospel and a prayer that believers be counted worthy and glorify Christ.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Paul urging the Thessalonians not to be shaken by claims that the day of Christ is present, stating a falling away and the “man of sin” must be revealed first. He describes this figure’s self-exaltation, satanic signs, deception, and coming judgment, notes a restraining power, gives thanks for their calling and sanctification, commands them to stand fast in received traditions, and prays for comfort and stability in good works.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s request for prayer for the spread of the word and deliverance from wicked men, affirming the Lord’s faithfulness. He commands believers to withdraw from disorderly brethren, cites his own labor as an example, and orders that unwilling workers not eat. He instructs busybodies to work quietly, urges perseverance in doing good, directs discipline without treating offenders as enemies, and closes with peace, a signed greeting, and a benediction.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records Paul greeting Timothy, urging him to remain in Ephesus and stop false doctrine, fables, and genealogies. It states the aim of the commandment is love from a pure heart, good conscience, and sincere faith. Paul explains lawful use of the law against sinners, recounts his past persecution and Christ’s mercy, and charges Timothy to fight faithfully, noting Hymenaeus and Alexander.

This chapter contains 15 verses and covers exhortations to offer prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving for all people, including rulers, so believers may live quietly and godly. It states God desires all to be saved, affirms one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gives himself as a ransom, and notes Paul’s commission to teach Gentiles. It instructs men to pray without anger and women to dress modestly, learn quietly, not teach or exercise authority over men, referencing Adam and Eve, and mentions salvation in childbearing with continuing faith, charity, holiness, and sobriety.

This chapter contains 16 verses and describes qualifications for bishops/overseers, including character, family leadership, teaching ability, and reputation. It also lists standards for deacons and their wives, requiring sobriety, honesty, and being tested before serving. Paul writes so Timothy knows proper conduct in the church of the living God, and it records a summary of the mystery of godliness concerning Christ’s manifestation, proclamation, belief, and ascension.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records a warning that some later depart from the faith through deceptive spirits and hypocritical teaching that forbids marriage and certain foods; it affirms food is to be received with thanksgiving and sanctified by God’s word and prayer. Paul instructs Timothy to teach these matters, reject profane fables, pursue godliness, set an example, attend to reading and doctrine, use his gift, and persevere in teaching.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records instructions on treating older and younger men and women with respect and purity, honoring “widows indeed,” and requiring families to support their own. It sets qualifications for widows supported by the church and urges younger widows to marry and manage households. It directs honoring and supporting ruling elders, handling accusations with witnesses, rebuking public sin, avoiding partiality, and not ordaining hastily; includes advice to use a little wine for infirmities.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records instructions for servants to honor masters, warnings against false teachers and quarrelsome disputing, and teaching that godliness with contentment is gain. It warns about desire for riches and the love of money, urges Timothy to pursue righteousness and fight the faith, and charges him to keep the commandment until Christ’s appearing. It instructs the rich to trust God, do good, and be generous, and to avoid profane babblings and false knowledge.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Paul’s greeting to Timothy, his prayers and desire to see him, and a reminder of Timothy’s faith from Lois and Eunice. Paul urges Timothy to stir up God’s gift, reject fear, and not be ashamed of Christ or Paul’s imprisonment. He summarizes God’s saving calling, Christ’s abolishing death, and Paul’s appointed ministry. He commands holding sound doctrine and notes Asia’s desertion, commending Onesiphorus for aid in Rome and Ephesus.

This chapter contains 26 verses and records Paul urging Timothy to be strong in grace, entrust teaching to faithful men, and endure hardship like a soldier, athlete, and farmer. Paul notes Christ’s resurrection, his own imprisonment, and a saying about suffering, reigning, and denial. Timothy is charged to avoid word disputes, study rightly, shun profane talk, reject Hymenaeus and Philetus’ error, depart from iniquity, pursue righteousness, and correct opponents gently.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records Paul warning Timothy that perilous last days bring widespread selfishness, vice, and a godliness form without power; Timothy is to avoid such people. It describes deceivers who infiltrate homes, resist truth like Jannes and Jambres, and are exposed. Paul recalls persecutions at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, states godly living brings persecution, urges perseverance in learned doctrine, and affirms Scripture’s divine inspiration and usefulness.

This chapter contains 22 verses and records Paul’s charge to Timothy to preach, correct, and endure amid people rejecting sound doctrine. Paul states his departure is near and he has kept the faith, expecting a crown of righteousness. He requests Timothy come soon, notes Demas leaving, names Crescens, Titus, Luke, Mark, and Tychicus, and asks for a cloak and parchments. He warns about Alexander, recounts abandonment at his defense, and sends greetings and travel notes.

This chapter contains 16 verses and records Paul’s greeting to Titus and his commission to organize the church in Crete. Paul instructs Titus to appoint elders in every city and lists qualifications for elders/bishops, including blameless conduct and sound doctrine. He warns about unruly deceivers, especially from the circumcision, who teach for gain, and commands sharp rebuke and rejection of Jewish fables and human commandments. It contrasts purity and defilement and notes professed faith denied by works.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Paul instructing Titus to teach sound doctrine and specific conduct for older men, older women, young women, young men, and servants, including sobriety, faithfulness, obedience, and good works. It states that God’s saving grace appears to all, training believers to deny ungodliness and live soberly and righteously while awaiting Jesus Christ’s appearing. It notes Christ’s self-giving to redeem and purify a people and commands Titus to exhort and rebuke with authority.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records Paul’s instructions to Titus: remind believers to submit to rulers, obey magistrates, avoid slander and quarrels, and show gentleness. It contrasts former sinful living with God’s mercy, salvation, regeneration, and justification through Jesus Christ and the Holy Ghost, urging continual good works. It warns to avoid disputes about the law and to reject a divisive person after admonitions. It includes travel plans to Nicopolis, help for Zenas and Apollos, and greetings.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Paul and Timothy’s greeting to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the house church, with thanksgiving for Philemon’s faith and love. Paul appeals for Onesimus, now useful, to be received as a beloved brother, offering to repay any debt. He requests lodging, expects release through prayers, and includes greetings from Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, ending with a grace benediction.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records God speaking formerly by prophets and now by his Son, appointed heir and agent of creation, who purges sins and sits at God’s right hand. It cites scriptures to show the Son’s superior name and throne above angels, angels’ worship of him, his role in founding earth and heavens, his unchanging nature, and angels as ministering spirits to heirs of salvation.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records an exhortation to heed the message of salvation confirmed by witnesses, signs, miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost. It states the world to come is not subjected to angels, quotes that mankind is set over God’s works, and says Jesus becomes lower than angels to suffer death for all. It describes Jesus sharing flesh and blood, defeating the devil’s power of death, delivering those in bondage, taking Abraham’s seed, becoming a merciful high priest, making reconciliation, and helping the tempted.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records an exhortation to consider Christ Jesus as Apostle and High Priest, faithful and greater than Moses, with believers as God’s house if they hold confidence. It quotes the warning “Today” not to harden hearts as Israel did in the wilderness. It urges mutual daily exhortation against unbelief and sin, and recalls that the wilderness generation fails to enter God’s rest because of unbelief.

This chapter contains 16 verses and covers exhortations to fear coming short of God’s promised rest, contrasting faith with unbelief and citing God’s seventh-day rest and David’s “Today” warning. It states a remaining rest for God’s people and urges diligence to enter it. It describes God’s word as discerning and all creatures exposed to God. It presents Jesus as the great high priest, tempted yet sinless, urging confidence to seek mercy and grace.

This chapter contains 14 verses and describes the role of high priests taken from men to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, showing compassion and being called by God like Aaron. It records Christ being appointed Son and priest forever after the order of Melchisedec, offering prayers in suffering, learning obedience, and becoming the source of eternal salvation to those who obey. It rebukes dull hearing and urges maturity from milk to strong meat, with discernment of good and evil.

This chapter contains 20 verses and covers moving beyond foundational doctrines (repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment) toward maturity. It states the impossibility of restoring to repentance those who fall away after enlightenment, using land bearing fruit or thorns as analogy. It commends believers’ service, urges diligence and patience, recalls God’s oath to Abraham, and presents hope as an anchor where Jesus enters within the veil as eternal high priest after Melchisedec.

This chapter contains 28 verses and records Melchisedec as king of Salem and priest who blesses Abraham and receives tithes, showing his superiority to Levi. It argues that a priest arises after Melchisedec’s order, requiring a change of priesthood and law, and notes Jesus is from Judah and made priest by oath forever. It contrasts mortal Levitical priests with Jesus’ unchangeable priesthood, intercession, and once-for-all self-offering.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records that Jesus is high priest seated in heaven, ministering in the true tabernacle. It contrasts earthly priests who offer sacrifices under the law and serve a shadowy pattern shown to Moses. It states Christ mediates a better covenant with better promises, quotes the promised new covenant with Israel and Judah, and declares the first covenant old and ready to vanish.

This chapter contains 28 verses and describes the first covenant’s tabernacle layout and priestly duties, including the high priest entering the Holiest once yearly with blood. It states that gifts and rituals cannot perfect the conscience. It presents Christ as high priest and mediator of the new testament, entering once with his own blood for eternal redemption. It recalls Moses dedicating the covenant with blood, notes remission requires shedding of blood, contrasts earthly patterns with heaven, and mentions judgment, Christ’s one sacrifice, and his future appearing.

This chapter contains 39 verses and covers the limits of repeated Mosaic sacrifices, stating animal blood cannot remove sins, and records Christ’s coming to do God’s will and offer one sacrifice, then sit at God’s right hand. It cites the new covenant with laws written in hearts and sins remembered no more. It urges believers to draw near, hold faith, love, good works, and assembly, warns against wilful sin and judgment, recalls past persecutions, and calls for endurance and faith.

This chapter contains 40 verses and describes faith as assurance of unseen things, citing elders as examples. It recounts Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, and patriarchal blessings of Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. It covers Moses’ choices, the Passover, the Red Sea, Jericho, and Rahab, then lists judges, kings, prophets, victories, deliverances, persecutions, martyrdoms, and awaiting promises.

This chapter contains 29 verses and describes exhortations to run the race by laying aside sin and looking to Jesus who endured the cross. It explains God’s chastening of sons and urges endurance, straight paths, peace, and holiness, avoiding bitterness and immorality like Esau. It contrasts Sinai’s fearsome scene with heavenly Zion, the new covenant, and Jesus’ sprinkled blood, warning not to refuse God’s voice and noting a final shaking and an unshakable kingdom.

This chapter contains 25 verses and covers exhortations to continue brotherly love, show hospitality, remember prisoners, honor marriage, avoid covetousness, and trust God’s help. It urges respect for spiritual leaders and avoidance of strange doctrines. It references Jesus suffering outside the gate, seeking a future city, offering praise and doing good. The writer requests prayer, mentions Timothy’s release, sends greetings, and gives a benediction.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records James’s greeting to the scattered twelve tribes, exhorting joy and endurance in trials, prayer for wisdom in faith, and humility for poor and rich. It states temptation arises from personal lust leading to sin and death, while good gifts come from God. It commands swift hearing, restrained speech and anger, doing the word, controlling the tongue, caring for orphans and widows, and remaining unstained by the world.

This chapter contains 26 verses and covers warnings against showing favoritism to the rich over the poor in the assembly, calling such partiality sin. It cites the royal law to love one’s neighbor and teaches that breaking one point makes one a transgressor, urging speech and action under the law of liberty and mercy. It argues faith without works is dead, using examples of aiding the needy, Abraham offering Isaac, and Rahab helping messengers.

This chapter contains 18 verses and covers warnings against many becoming teachers and the stricter judgment involved. It describes the tongue’s power using images of a bit, rudder, and fire, saying it is hard to tame and can bless God while cursing people. It contrasts bitter envy and strife with wisdom shown by meek works, and lists traits of earthly versus heavenly wisdom, ending with righteousness sown in peace by peacemakers.

This chapter contains 17 verses and covers the source of conflicts in lusts, improper motives in prayer, and the warning that friendship with the world opposes God. It commands submission to God, resisting the devil, cleansing hands, purifying hearts, mourning, and humility. It forbids speaking evil and judging others, citing one lawgiver. It warns against boasting about future plans and defines sin as neglecting known good.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records warnings to rich oppressors about coming judgment, hoarded wealth, and withheld wages. It commands believers to be patient for the Lord’s coming, avoid grumbling, and follow examples of prophets and Job. It forbids swearing oaths, instructs prayer in affliction and praise in joy, and directs elders to pray and anoint the sick. It includes confession, effective prayer, Elijah’s prayers about rain, and restoring erring sinners.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Peter’s address to scattered believers in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen by God and sanctified by the Spirit. It describes new birth and an imperishable heavenly inheritance through Jesus’ resurrection, and endurance under trials. It notes prophets and angels concerning salvation. It commands sober hope, holiness, reverent conduct, and brotherly love, citing redemption by Christ’s blood and the enduring word preached in the gospel.

This chapter contains 25 verses and covers exhortations to lay aside malice and related sins and to desire the word. It describes believers coming to Christ the living cornerstone, being built as a spiritual house and priesthood, and contrasts belief with stumbling at the word. It identifies them as a chosen people and urges abstaining from lusts and living honorably among Gentiles. It commands submission to rulers, honoring others, and servants’ obedience, and it records Christ’s sinless suffering, bearing sins, and shepherding the restored.

This chapter contains 22 verses and covers instructions for wives to submit and for husbands to honor their wives; commands to be unified, compassionate, and to bless rather than retaliate. It urges guarding speech, doing good, seeking peace, and trusting God amid suffering for righteousness, with readiness to answer for hope. It recounts Christ’s suffering, proclamation to spirits in prison, Noah’s ark, baptism, and Christ’s exaltation.

This chapter contains 19 verses and covers arming oneself with Christ’s mindset in suffering, turning from former lusts and idolatry, and awaiting judgment of the living and the dead. It mentions the gospel preached to the dead, urges sobriety, prayer, charity, hospitality, and stewardship of spiritual gifts. It addresses fiery trials and reproach for Christ’s name, forbids suffering for wrongdoing, and calls sufferers to entrust their souls to God while doing good.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records Peter’s exhortations to elders to shepherd God’s flock willingly, without greed or domination, and to be examples. It commands younger believers to submit, and all to practice humility, casting cares on God. It warns to be sober and vigilant against the devil and to resist steadfast in faith amid shared afflictions, with a promise of strengthening after suffering. It notes Silvanus as messenger, sends greetings from Babylon and Marcus, and instructs loving greetings and peace.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records Peter addressing believers with shared faith, extending grace and peace through knowing God and Jesus. It states God gives promises for life and godliness, urges adding virtues to faith, and exhorts diligence to make calling sure. Peter plans reminders before death, cites eyewitness testimony on the holy mount, and affirms prophecy comes from God, not private interpretation or human will.

This chapter contains 22 verses and warns of false teachers who introduce heresies, exploit others, and face certain judgment. It cites past examples: sinful angels cast into chains, the flood with Noah preserved, and Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed while Lot is delivered. It describes their immoral, covetous conduct, compares them to Balaam, and states that returning to corruption after knowing Christ is worse.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records Peter’s second letter urging remembrance of prophets and apostolic commands, warning that scoffers question the Lord’s coming. It cites creation and the flood, and states the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire at judgment. It explains the Lord’s timing and patience, describes the day of the Lord’s sudden arrival and cosmic dissolution, anticipates new heavens and a new earth, exhorts holiness, references Paul’s letters, warns against distortion and error, and commands growth in grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ.

This chapter contains 10 verses and records the writer’s eyewitness testimony of the manifested Word of life and eternal life, declared to bring fellowship with the Father and Jesus Christ and to make readers’ joy full. It states that God is light with no darkness, warns against claiming fellowship while walking in darkness, and teaches walking in light and Jesus’ blood cleansing sin. It rejects claims of sinlessness, commands confession, and affirms forgiveness and cleansing.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records John’s exhortation not to sin and states that Jesus Christ is an advocate and propitiation for sins. It links knowing God with keeping commandments and walking as Christ walked, and contrasts love versus hatred of a brother. It addresses children, fathers, and young men, warns against loving the world, mentions many antichrists, denies false teachers, urges abiding in received teaching and anointing, and calls for righteousness and confidence at Christ’s coming.

This chapter contains 24 verses and describes believers as God’s children and future likeness to Christ, calls for purity and defines sin as lawlessness. It contrasts practicing righteousness with sin as of the devil, and urges love for one another, citing Cain’s murder. It warns of the world’s hatred, equates hate with murder, commands practical aid, and links confidence in prayer to keeping commandments, believing in Jesus, and the Spirit’s indwelling.

This chapter contains 21 verses and covers testing spirits amid false prophets, identifying God’s Spirit by confessing Jesus Christ come in the flesh, and distinguishing truth from error and antichrist. It records exhortations to love one another, states that God is love, and notes the Father sending the Son as Savior and propitiation. It describes God dwelling in believers by the Spirit, perfect love casting out fear, and commands loving one’s brother.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records that belief in Jesus as Christ and Son of God identifies those born of God, who love God and keep his commandments, overcoming the world by faith. It presents witnesses of Spirit, water, and blood, and God’s testimony of the Son granting eternal life. It states confidence in prayer according to God’s will, guidance about praying for a sin not unto death, assurance against the wicked one, and a warning to avoid idols.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the elder’s letter to the elect lady and her children, offering grace, mercy, and peace. He rejoices that some walk in truth, urges love and obedience to God’s commandments, and warns against deceivers denying Christ’s coming in the flesh. He instructs not to receive or support such teachers, seeks a full reward, plans a face-to-face visit, and sends greetings.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records the elder’s letter to Gaius, expressing love in truth and wishing him health. It reports testimony that Gaius walks in truth and commends his hospitality to traveling brethren and strangers sent for the Name’s sake. It urges receiving such workers. It describes Diotrephes refusing the elder and the brethren and expelling those who receive them. It commends Demetrius and closes with plans to visit and greetings.

This chapter contains 25 verses and records Jude’s greeting and blessing, an exhortation to contend for the faith, and a warning about ungodly intruders who deny the Lord and corrupt conduct. It recalls judgments on unbelieving Israel, rebellious angels, and Sodom and Gomorrah, and cites Michael’s dispute with the devil. It compares the deceivers to Cain, Balaam, and Korah, quotes Enoch on coming judgment, urges believers to build faith, pray, show mercy, and ends with a doxology.

This chapter contains 20 verses and records John introducing the revelation given by God through an angel, blessing readers who keep it, and addressing seven churches in Asia. From Patmos John hears a trumpet-like voice commanding him to write to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. He sees seven candlesticks and the Son of man holding seven stars, declares his authority over death, and explains stars and candlesticks.

This chapter contains 29 verses and records messages to the churches in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamos, and Thyatira. It notes each church’s works and challenges, calls for repentance or faithfulness, warns of judgment (removing a candlestick, prison, fighting with the sword, tribulation), mentions Nicolaitans, Balaam, Antipas, and “Jezebel,” and promises rewards to overcomers (tree of life, crown of life, hidden manna, white stone, authority over nations, morning star).

This chapter contains 22 verses and records messages to the churches in Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. Sardis is told to watch, strengthen what remains, remember, hold fast, and repent, with promises to overcomers and warning of sudden coming. Philadelphia receives an open door, protection from testing, and promises of a pillar and new names. Laodicea is rebuked for lukewarmness and self-sufficiency, urged to seek refined gold, white raiment, and eyesalve, repent, open the door, and overcome.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records John being called through an open door into heaven and seeing a throne with one seated, described with jasper and sardine and a rainbow. It describes twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns, lightning and thunder, seven lamps, a sea of glass, and four living creatures praising God day and night, prompting elders to worship and cast crowns.

This chapter contains 14 verses and records John seeing a scroll with seven seals in the hand of the One on the throne, and a strong angel asking who is worthy to open it. None is found until an elder points to the Lion of Judah/Root of David, seen as a slain Lamb. The Lamb takes the scroll, receives worship and a new song from the four living creatures and twenty-four elders, is praised by innumerable angels, and all creation worships the One on the throne and the Lamb.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records the Lamb opening the first six seals. Four horsemen appear on white, red, black, and pale horses, bringing conquest, warfare, scarcity, and death over part of the earth. Souls of martyrs under the altar cry for judgment and receive white robes. A great earthquake and cosmic disturbances occur, and all classes hide, fearing the wrath of the Lamb.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records John seeing four angels restraining the earth’s winds, and another angel commanding no harm until God’s servants are sealed. It lists 144,000 sealed from twelve tribes of Israel. John then sees an innumerable multitude from all nations before the throne and the Lamb, worshiping. An elder identifies them as coming from great tribulation, serving in God’s temple, sheltered from hunger and heat, led by the Lamb.

This chapter contains 13 verses and records the opening of the seventh seal and a half-hour silence in heaven. Seven angels receive trumpets, and another angel offers incense with the prayers of the saints, then casts fire to earth causing thunder, lightning, and an earthquake. The first four trumpets bring hail and fire with blood, a burning mountain in the sea, the star Wormwood poisoning waters, and darkness on sun, moon, and stars. An angel announces three coming woes.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records the fifth and sixth trumpet judgments. A star receives the key to the bottomless pit, releasing smoke and locusts that torment unsealed people for five months under Abaddon/Apollyon. Then four angels bound at the Euphrates are loosed to kill a third of humanity by an immense cavalry with fire, smoke, and brimstone. Survivors do not repent of idolatry, murders, sorceries, fornication, or thefts.

This chapter contains 11 verses and records John seeing a mighty angel descend from heaven with an open little book, standing on sea and earth and crying out as seven thunders speak. John is commanded to seal up the thunders’ words. The angel swears by the Creator that time is no longer and that God’s mystery is finished when the seventh angel sounds. John takes and eats the book, sweet then bitter, and is told to prophesy to many peoples and kings.

This chapter contains 19 verses and records John measuring God’s temple while the outer court is left to Gentiles for 42 months. It covers two witnesses prophesying 1,260 days with power to judge and protect themselves, their death by the beast, public exposure, resurrection, and ascension, followed by an earthquake killing 7,000. The seventh trumpet sounds; heavenly voices, elders’ worship, judgment and rewards are announced, and God’s heavenly temple opens with the ark and signs.

This chapter contains 17 verses and records signs in heaven of a woman clothed with the sun who bears a male child, and a red dragon seeking to devour him. The child is caught up to God, and the woman flees to the wilderness for 1,260 days. War occurs in heaven as Michael casts Satan and his angels to earth. A heavenly voice announces the accuser’s defeat. The dragon persecutes the woman, sends a flood, the earth swallows it, and he makes war on her remnant who keep God’s commandments and hold Jesus’ testimony.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records John seeing a beast from the sea with seven heads and ten horns, empowered by the dragon, speaking blasphemies, warring with saints, and receiving worldwide worship for forty-two months. A second beast from the earth performs wonders, directs worship of the first, and enforces an image. It requires a mark to buy or sell and gives the number 666.

This chapter contains 20 verses and describes the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with 144,000 bearing the Father’s name and singing a new song. It records three angels proclaiming the everlasting gospel, announcing Babylon’s fall, and warning against worshiping the beast and receiving its mark. It blesses those who die in the Lord, notes saints keeping God’s commandments, and depicts harvest and winepress judgments on the earth.

This chapter contains 8 verses and describes John seeing seven angels in heaven with the seven last plagues. He sees a sea of glass mingled with fire and victors over the beast standing with harps, singing the song of Moses and of the Lamb about God’s works and judgments. The heavenly temple opens; angels receive seven golden vials of wrath, and the temple fills with smoke until the plagues are completed.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records seven angels pouring out bowls of God’s wrath: sores on those with the beast’s mark, sea and waters becoming blood, scorching heat, darkness on the beast’s throne, Euphrates dried to prepare kings of the east, unclean spirits gathering rulers to Armageddon, and a final outpouring bringing “It is done,” earthquake, Babylon judged, islands and mountains removed, and great hail as people blaspheme and do not repent.

This chapter contains 18 verses and records an angel showing John the judgment of a woman called Mystery Babylon seated on many waters, riding a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns. The angel explains the waters as peoples, the heads as seven mountains and seven kings, and the horns as ten kings who give power to the beast. They war with the Lamb and are overcome. The ten horns later destroy the woman; she represents a ruling city.

This chapter contains 24 verses and records an angel announcing Babylon’s fall and uncleanness, and a heavenly voice calling God’s people to come out to avoid her plagues. It describes her sins, judgment in one day, and burning. Kings, merchants, and seafarers lament the loss of trade and luxuries. Heaven rejoices; an angel symbolizes Babylon’s permanent overthrow, ending her music, crafts, light, and weddings, and notes bloodguilt for prophets and saints.

This chapter contains 21 verses and records heavenly praise for God’s righteous judgments and the fall of the great whore, the marriage of the Lamb and the blessed invited, and a command to worship God. John sees heaven opened and a rider on a white horse called Faithful and True, the Word of God, leading heavenly armies to judge and war. The beast and false prophet are cast into the lake of fire; remaining armies are slain.

This chapter contains 15 verses and records an angel binding Satan and sealing him in the bottomless pit for a thousand years, during which martyrs reign with Christ in the first resurrection. After Satan is released, he gathers Gog and Magog against the saints, but fire from heaven destroys them and the devil is cast into the lake of fire. It then describes the great white throne judgment, the opening of books and the book of life, and the casting of death, hell, and the unlisted into the lake of fire.

This chapter contains 27 verses and records John’s vision of a new heaven and new earth and the new Jerusalem descending from God. A voice declares God dwells with humanity, removes tears, and ends death and pain. God names himself Alpha and Omega, promises the water of life and inheritance to overcomers, and assigns the wicked to the lake of fire. An angel shows and measures the city’s gates, foundations, materials, light, open gates, and exclusion of the defiled.

This chapter contains 21 verses and describes the river of life and tree of life in the city where God and the Lamb reign, with no curse or night. An angel affirms the prophecy as true and imminent; John is told to worship God and not seal the book. Jesus declares his soon coming and judgment, blesses commandment keepers, excludes evildoers, invites all to take the water of life, warns against altering the prophecy, and closes with a final promise and benediction.
